questions.stem: Which two families of compound react to make an ester?

options.text: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid
options.explanation: Those are exactly the two reactants the esterification recipe calls for.
That pairing makes an alcohol by hydration, not an ester.
That pairing releases carbon dioxide and builds a salt, not an ester.
Substitution with halogens builds haloalkanes, a different family.

questions.stem: What else is produced alongside the ester during esterification?

options.explanation: The reaction is a joining that always pays for itself with water.
One -H and one -OH leave the reactants as a water molecule for every ester link made.
Hydrogen belongs to acid-metal reactions, not to esterification.
No carbonate is present, so no carbon dioxide can form.

questions.stem: Which catalyst is used when ethanol and ethanoic acid make ethyl ethanoate?

options.explanation: Enzymes belong to fermentation, not to ester-making.

options.text: No catalyst is needed at all
options.explanation: Without the acid catalyst the reaction is impractically slow.
The strong acid catalyses the joining without being consumed.
Phosphoric acid catalyses ethene hydration, a different process.

questions.stem: Which arrangement marks a compound as an ester?

options.explanation: That is the carboxylic acid group, the reactant rather than the product.
A lone -OH marks an alcohol.
A C=C marks an alkene and plays no part in the ester group.

options.text: A -COO- link sitting between two carbon chains
options.explanation: The R-COO-R arrangement is the ester signature.

questions.stem: Which ester is produced from ethanol and ethanoic acid?

options.explanation: The alcohol gives ethyl and the acid gives ethanoate, in that order.
Methyl would need methanol, one carbon shorter than ethanol.
Methanoate would need methanoic acid, one carbon shorter than ethanoic.
Propyl would need propanol, one carbon longer than ethanol.

questions.stem: State the name given to the reaction between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid that makes an ester.
State the small molecule released when the alcohol and the acid join to make the ester.
questions.modelAnswer: A molecule of water is released as the reactants join.

questions.stem: An ester formula is written CH3COOC2H5. Explain what the two parts on either side of the COO group represent.
questions.misconceptionClass: two chains around the ester link
questions.modelAnswer: The CH3CO part comes from the carboxylic acid chain and the C2H5 part comes from the alcohol chain, joined through the ester link.

questions.stem: Propanol is reacted with ethanoic acid in the presence of the usual catalyst. Name the ester produced.
Which ester forms from methanol and ethanoic acid?

options.explanation: That ester needs ethanol, one carbon longer than methanol.
One-carbon alcohol gives methyl, two-carbon acid gives ethanoate.
Both halves are shifted: the reactants are reversed in size.
The acid half stays ethanoate because ethanoic acid supplies it.

questions.stem: An ester is named propyl methanoate. Which two reactants made it?

options.explanation: Ethanol lends ethyl, not propyl.
The acid half would then read propanoate, not methanoate.
Propyl points to a three-carbon alcohol and methanoate to the one-carbon acid.
That pair would be named methyl propanoate, the mirror mix-up.

questions.stem: Why are esters chosen for perfumes?

options.text: They are the cheapest liquids available
options.explanation: Cost is not the stated reason; smell and volatility are.

options.text: They are completely unreactive on skin
options.explanation: Inertness is not the property being exploited in perfumery.
Solvent power over salts is irrelevant to perfume use.

options.text: They are volatile with distinctive pleasant smells
options.explanation: Easy evaporation carries the scent, and the smells are exactly the sweet kind wanted.

questions.stem: In the ester name butyl propanoate, what does the butyl part describe?

options.text: The four-carbon chain donated by the alcohol
options.explanation: The yl segment always reports the alcohol side of the ester.

options.text: The chain donated by the acid
options.explanation: The acid side is always reported in the oate segment.
Water takes no part in ester naming.
Catalysts never appear in the product name.

questions.stem: Which statement about the volatility of esters is correct?

options.text: Volatility makes them gases at room temperature
options.explanation: They are described as oily liquids that evaporate easily, not as gases.

options.text: Their low boiling points let vapours reach the nose readily
options.explanation: Volatility means easy evaporation, which delivers the scent efficiently.

options.text: They never evaporate at room temperature
options.explanation: Volatility means precisely that they do evaporate readily.
Esters boil below water in many cases, which is why they smell at all.

questions.stem: Name the ester formed when pentanol reacts with butanoic acid.
State the ending that the alcohol-derived part of an ester name always carries.
questions.modelAnswer: The part from the alcohol always ends in yl.

questions.stem: Explain why ethyl ethanoate, rather than the reactants it was made from, is chosen to carry a fruity scent in a food flavouring.
questions.modelAnswer: Esters are volatile liquids with distinctive sweet smells, so the ester itself carries the fruity aroma while the acid and alcohol do not.

questions.stem: An ester is named methyl butanoate. State which acid family member contributed its chain to this ester.
questions.misconceptionClass: reading the acid from the oate part
questions.modelAnswer: The acid partner is butanoic acid — the butanoate part of the name comes from the carboxylic acid.
